title: Vaginal birth
what: Having your baby the natural way. Contractions open the cervix, then pushing helps the baby come out.
why: Usually at 37 to 42 weeks of pregnancy, when the baby is ready to be born.
duration: a first birth usually takes longer, often 8 to 12 hours or more; later births are usually shorter
tell_doctor: Heart disease, blood pressure problems, or diabetes
How your past births went, if you had any
If you want pain relief during labor

prepare.title: Pregnancy records
prepare.text: From 30 to 32 weeks, carry your pregnancy records and ID with you.

prepare.title: Hospital bag
prepare.text: Pack it ahead of time: things for you and the baby. The hospital will give you a list.

prepare.title: When to go
prepare.text: Usually when contractions are regular, about every 5 to 10 minutes, or your water breaks. Check with your doctor.

prepare.title: Pain relief
prepare.text: Ask your doctor ahead of time about pain relief options during labor.

steps: At admission, you are examined and the baby's heartbeat is checked
Contractions slowly get stronger and closer together
The doctor and midwife check how the cervix opens and listen to the baby's heart
When the cervix is fully open, pushing starts. The midwife shows you how to push
The baby is born and placed on your chest
A few minutes later, the placenta comes out
feel: Contractions are strong pain in waves, with rest in between
Moving, breathing, and changing position can help
When pushing, strong pressure down below
If the pain is hard to bear, say so. Pain relief will be discussed
after: You and the baby are watched in the delivery room for a few hours
Bleeding usually lasts up to 6 weeks
You usually go home after 1 to 3 days
See your gynecologist when your doctor tells you
red_flags: Before birth: bleeding, green or brown water, or the baby moving less. Call emergency services
A bad headache, spots before your eyes, or swelling: call emergency services
After birth: heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour
A fever over 38 degrees, chest pain, shortness of breath, or one swollen leg

faq.q: How do I know labor has started?
faq.a: Contractions become regular and closer together, or your water breaks. Then call your doctor or go to the hospital.

faq.q: Can I have pain relief during labor?
faq.a: Yes. There are different options, including a shot in the back called an epidural. Talk with your doctor ahead of time.

faq.q: Can my partner be there for the birth?
faq.a: Many hospitals allow it. Check your hospital's rules ahead of time.
